A hash map is a data structure that stores key-value pairs and allows you to look up a value quickly given its key, typically in constant time regardless of how many items it holds. The central idea is to avoid searching through data by instead computing, in advance, exactly where each item should live.

When you insert a pair, the map first passes the key through a hash function, which converts it into a number. A good hash function spreads keys uniformly across the possible range, so that even similar keys produce very different outputs. That number is then reduced to fit within the bounds of the map's underlying array, usually by taking it modulo the array's size, and the result serves as the index where the value will be stored. Because the same key always produces the same index, retrieving a value later is simply a matter of repeating the calculation and going straight to that spot.

The complication is that two different keys can occasionally hash to the same index, a situation called a collision. Maps handle this in a couple of common ways. One approach, chaining, keeps a small list at each array slot, so colliding entries simply coexist in that list and a lookup scans it briefly. The other, open addressing, keeps everything in the array itself and, when a slot is taken, probes onward to find the next available one, using a pattern like checking successive positions or jumping by increasing steps. Either way, collisions are kept rare by the quality of the hash function, so these extra steps stay short.

As entries accumulate, the array fills up and collisions become more frequent, which would degrade performance. To prevent this, the map monitors its load factor, the ratio of entries to available slots, and when it crosses a threshold the map rehashes: it allocates a larger array and redistributes every existing entry according to the new size.
